Moles of gas: \(n = \frac{P_{1}V_{1}}{RT} = \frac{(0.5\times10^{6})(20\times10^{-3})}{8.314\times600} \approx 2\) mol.

For an ideal gas at constant temperature the internal energy and enthalpy depend only on \(T\), so \(\Delta U = 0\) and \(\Delta H = 0\).

Reversible isothermal work: \(w = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{P_{1}}{P_{2}} = -2.303\times2\times8.314\times600\times\log\frac{0.5}{0.2}\).

\(\log 2.5 = \log5 - \log2 = 0.6989 - 0.3010 = 0.3979\), so \(w = -2.303\times9976.8\times0.3979 \approx -9.1\times10^{3}\) J \(= -9.1\) kJ.

From the first law \(\Delta U = q + w = 0 \Rightarrow q = -w = +9.1\) kJ.

Hence \(w = -9.1\) kJ, \(\Delta U = 0\), \(\Delta H = 0\), \(q = +9.1\) kJ.

A carbanion is stabilised when its lone pair sits in an orbital of higher s-character, because s-orbitals are closer to the nucleus and hold the negative charge more tightly.

Hybridisation of the carbanion carbon: \(CH \equiv C^{-}\) is sp (50% s), \(CH_{2}=CH^{-}\) is \(sp^{2}\) (33% s), \(CH_{3}-CH_{2}^{-}\) is \(sp^{3}\) (25% s).

Therefore stability follows \(CH \equiv C^{-} > CH_{2}=CH^{-} > CH_{3}-CH_{2}^{-}\), which is also why terminal alkynes are the most acidic of the three parent hydrocarbons.

For an ideal solution, \(P = x_{A}P_{A}^{\circ} + x_{B}P_{B}^{\circ}\).

Stage 1 (2 mol A, 3 mol B, total 5): \(\frac{2}{5}P_{A}^{\circ} + \frac{3}{5}P_{B}^{\circ} = 320 \Rightarrow 2P_{A}^{\circ} + 3P_{B}^{\circ} = 1600\).

Stage 2 (3 mol A, 4 mol B, total 7): \(\frac{3}{7}P_{A}^{\circ} + \frac{4}{7}P_{B}^{\circ} = 328.6 \Rightarrow 3P_{A}^{\circ} + 4P_{B}^{\circ} = 2300.2\).

Multiply the first by 3 and the second by 2: \(6P_{A}^{\circ} + 9P_{B}^{\circ} = 4800\) and \(6P_{A}^{\circ} + 8P_{B}^{\circ} = 4600.4\). Subtracting gives \(P_{B}^{\circ} \approx 200\) mm Hg.

Then \(2P_{A}^{\circ} = 1600 - 600 = 1000 \Rightarrow P_{A}^{\circ} = 500\) mm Hg.

So \(P_{A}^{\circ} = 500\) and \(P_{B}^{\circ} = 200\) mm Hg respectively.

The bracketed data fix the starting material: \(76.6\%\ C,\ 6.38\%\ H\) and hence \(17.02\%\ O\) give a mole ratio \(6.38 : 6.38 : 1.064 = 6:6:1\), i.e. \(C_{6}H_{6}O\); vapour density 47 gives \(M = 94\), which matches \(C_{6}H_{6}O\) exactly. So compound \(x\) is phenol.

Phenol with \(CO_{2}\)/NaOH at \(120^{\circ}C\) and high pressure, followed by \(H_{3}O^{+}\), is the Kolbe-Schmitt reaction, giving salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid) as compound \(y\). Compound \(y\) still carries a phenolic \(-OH\), which is why it gives the characteristic violet colour with neutral \(FeCl_{3}\).

Checking the statements: (A) both phenol and salicylic acid dissolve in NaOH - true. (B) salicylic acid has a \(-COOH\) group, so it dissolves in \(NaHCO_{3}\) with evolution of \(CO_{2}\) - true. (D) both are aromatic and burn with a sooty flame - true. (C) phenol has \(pK_{a} \approx 10\) while salicylic acid has \(pK_{a} \approx 3\) (carboxyl plus intramolecular hydrogen bonding in the carboxylate), so \(y\) is far more acidic than \(x\) - this statement is FALSE.

Benzene with \(Br_{2}/FeBr_{3}\) undergoes electrophilic bromination to give bromobenzene (A). \(-Br\) is deactivating but ortho/para directing, so nitration with conc. \(HNO_{3}\)/conc. \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) gives 1-bromo-2-nitrobenzene and 1-bromo-4-nitrobenzene as the pair B and C.

These two isomers have very close boiling points (about \(261^{\circ}C\) and \(256^{\circ}C\)), so simple distillation cannot resolve them. Neither isomer sublimes, and steam distillation would need one isomer to be appreciably steam-volatile through intramolecular hydrogen bonding, which is impossible here since there is no \(-OH\) or \(-NH\) group.

A mixture of liquids whose boiling points differ by only a few degrees is separated by fractional distillation.

pH 9 at \(25^{\circ}C\) means \(pOH = 5\). For a basic buffer, \(pOH = pK_{b} + \log\frac{[\,BH^{+}]}{[B]}\).

So \(5 = 5.699 + \log\frac{[BH^{+}]}{[B]} \Rightarrow \log\frac{[BH^{+}]}{[B]} = -0.699 \Rightarrow \frac{[BH^{+}]}{[B]} = \frac{1}{5}\).

HCl is the limiting reagent; it converts an equal number of moles of B into \(BH^{+}\). Since both solutions are 0.02 M, moles are proportional to volumes: \(BH^{+} \propto x\) and leftover \(B \propto (y-x)\).

\(\frac{x}{y-x} = \frac{1}{5} \Rightarrow y = 6x\). With \(x + y = 100\), \(7x = 100 \Rightarrow x = 14.3\) mL and \(y = 85.7\) mL.

Hence \(x = 14.3\) mL of HCl and \(y = 85.7\) mL of base B.

For a first order reaction, \(t = \frac{2.303}{k}\log\frac{[A]_{0}}{[A]}\).

Decomposition to one-eighth: \(t_{1/8} = \frac{2.303}{k}\log 8 = \frac{2.303}{k}(3\log 2) = \frac{2.303}{k}(0.9)\).

Decomposition to one-tenth: \(t_{1/10} = \frac{2.303}{k}\log 10 = \frac{2.303}{k}(1)\).

Therefore \(\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}} = 0.9\) and \(\frac{t_{1/8}}{t_{1/10}}\times 10 = 9\).

For \(EH_{3}\) with E = N, P, As, Sb:

(A) The E-H bond enthalpy falls steadily as the size of E increases, so thermal stability decreases down the group: \(NH_{3} > PH_{3} > AsH_{3} > SbH_{3}\). CORRECT.

(B) The lone pair becomes more diffuse and less available for donation as the central atom gets larger, so basicity decreases down the group: \(NH_{3} > PH_{3} > AsH_{3} > SbH_{3}\). CORRECT.

(C) Weaker E-H bonds are broken more easily, so the hydrides become progressively better reducing agents down the group. CORRECT.

(D) Boiling points do NOT increase monotonically. \(NH_{3}\) is anomalously high because of intermolecular hydrogen bonding, giving the order \(PH_{3} < AsH_{3} < NH_{3} < SbH_{3}\). INCORRECT.

Hence (A), (B) and (C) only.

The Griess-Ilosvay test is the standard qualitative test for the nitrite ion and uses exactly the two reagents named: sulphanilic acid and \(\alpha\)-naphthylamine in acidic solution. Statement I is true.

The chemistry is also correctly described. Acidified nitrite generates nitrous acid, which diazotises the \(-NH_{2}\) group of sulphanilic acid to the corresponding diazonium ion at low temperature. This diazonium ion then couples at the electron-rich position of \(\alpha\)-naphthylamine to give a red azo dye, which is what signals the presence of nitrite. Statement II is true and it correctly explains Statement I.

Taking the four schemes in turn.

(A) Nitration of the phenyl carbamate \(PhNH-CO-O-Ph\): of the two rings, the one bearing the amide nitrogen \((-NH-CO-)\) is the more strongly activated, because nitrogen is a better electron donor than the ester oxygen of \(-O-CO-\). Nitration should therefore occur para on the N-aryl ring, not on the O-aryl ring as drawn. Incorrect.

(B) Gabriel phthalimide synthesis: the phthalimide anion is a nucleophile and displaces halide by an \(S_{N}2\) pathway. Aryl halides do not undergo \(S_{N}2\), so potassium phthalimide with an aryl halide will not deliver aniline. This is the standard limitation of the Gabriel synthesis. Incorrect.

(C) Benzylamine with \(CHCl_{3}\)/alcoholic KOH gives benzyl isocyanide by the carbylamine reaction, which is fine, but reduction of an isocyanide with \(Sn/HCl\) adds hydrogen to the \(N \equiv C\) unit and gives the SECONDARY amine \(PhCH_{2}NHCH_{3}\), not the primary amine shown. Incorrect.

(D) Propanamide with \(Br_{2}\) and 4 equivalents of KOH is Hofmann bromamide degradation. The amide is converted through the N-bromoamide and an isocyanate to an amine with ONE carbon fewer, giving ethylamine, and 4 equivalents of base is exactly the stoichiometric requirement. Correct.

Hence (D) is the correct reaction.

Reading the pentapeptide from the free \(-NH_{2}\) end on the left to the \(-COOH\) end on the right, the side chains attached to the successive alpha-carbons are:

1st residue: \(-CH(OH)CH_{3}\) which is threonine; 2nd residue: \(-CH_{2}OH\) which is serine; 3rd residue: \(-CH_{2}COOH\) which is aspartic acid; 4th residue: \(-H\) which is glycine; 5th residue: \(-CH_{3}\) which is alanine.

So the sequence is Thr - Ser - Asp - Gly - Ala.

Of these five, serine, aspartic acid, glycine and alanine are all non-essential amino acids that the human body can synthesise. Threonine cannot be synthesised and must be supplied in the diet, so the essential amino acid \(Y\) is threonine.

Styrene with HBr in the presence of benzoyl peroxide undergoes anti-Markovnikov (peroxide effect) radical addition.

(A) Bromine radical adds to the terminal \(CH_{2}\) so that the resulting radical \(Ph\dot{C}H-CH_{2}Br\) is benzylic and resonance stabilised by the ring. The reaction indeed proceeds through the more stable radical intermediate. CORRECT.

(B) Peroxide homolysis gives \(PhCOO\cdot\), which loses \(CO_{2}\) to give \(Ph\cdot\); these radicals abstract hydrogen from HBr to generate BROMINE radicals, which are the chain carriers. The peroxide does not generate a hydrogen radical. INCORRECT.

(C) The phenyl radical produced from benzoyl peroxide abstracts H from HBr, so benzene is formed as a by-product alongside \(CO_{2}\). CORRECT.

(D) Anti-Markovnikov addition puts Br on the terminal carbon, giving \(PhCH_{2}CH_{2}Br\), 1-bromo-2-phenylethane. That is the MAJOR product, not the minor one. INCORRECT.

(E) Without peroxide the addition is ionic and Markovnikov, proceeding through the resonance stabilised benzylic carbocation \(Ph\overset{+}{C}H-CH_{3}\) to give 1-bromo-1-phenylethane. CORRECT.

Correct statements are (A), (C) and (E).

For the Balmer series the electron falls to \(n_{1} = 2\), so the wave number is \(\bar{\nu} = R\left(\frac{1}{2^{2}} - \frac{1}{n_{2}^{2}}\right)\) with \(n_{2} = 3, 4, 5, \ldots\)

\(n_{2}=3:\ R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{9}\right) = \frac{5R}{36}\)

\(n_{2}=4:\ R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{16}\right) = \frac{3R}{16}\)

\(n_{2}=5:\ R\left(\frac{1}{4}-\frac{1}{25}\right) = \frac{21R}{100}\)

All three members of set (A) are Balmer lines. The other sets contain values such as \(\frac{3R}{4}\) and \(\frac{8R}{9}\) (Lyman, \(n_{1}=1\)) and \(\frac{7R}{144}\) (Paschen, \(n_{1}=3\)).

Figure 1 shows the 2s orbital with a spherical nodal surface, i.e. a spherical shell on which the probability of finding the electron is zero.

A node is the place where the wave function itself vanishes and changes sign. In Figure 2, \(\psi_{2s}(x)\) starts positive at A, crosses the x-axis at B, becomes negative through the minimum at C, and is still negative (approaching zero from below) at D.

The only point where \(\psi_{2s} = 0\) with a sign change is B, so B represents the nodal surface. Note that C is a minimum, not a node, and D is merely a small negative value.

Hence the answer is B, which is option (A).

Period 4 runs from K and Ca through the 3d series Sc to Zn and then Ga, Ge, As, Se, Br, Kr.

Atomic radius decreases across a period as the effective nuclear charge rises, so the first member K has the largest atomic radius and the last true covalent member Br has the smallest.

Na and Cl belong to period 3 and Rb belongs to period 5, so those options are out on the period alone. Kr is excluded because its radius is quoted as a van der Waals radius, which is not comparable with the covalent radii of the other elements and is in fact larger than that of Br.

Hence highest is K and lowest is Br.

\(Ni(CO)_{4}\): nickel is in the zero oxidation state, \(3d^{8}4s^{2}\); CO is a strong field ligand, so the \(4s\) electrons pair into the \(3d\) set giving \(3d^{10}4s^{0}\). Hybridisation is \(sp^{3}\), the geometry is tetrahedral, there are no unpaired electrons and the complex is diamagnetic.

\([Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}\): \(Ni^{2+}\) is \(3d^{8}\); \(CN^{-}\) is a strong field ligand and pairs the two unpaired \(3d\) electrons, freeing a \(3d\) orbital for \(dsp^{2}\) hybridisation. The geometry is square planar and the complex is diamagnetic.

\([NiCl_{4}]^{2-}\): \(Cl^{-}\) is a weak field ligand and does not force pairing, so \(Ni^{2+}\) keeps two unpaired \(3d\) electrons. Hybridisation is \(sp^{3}\), the geometry is tetrahedral and the complex is paramagnetic with \(\mu = \sqrt{8}\) BM.

Hence \(Ni(CO)_{4}\) and \([Ni(CN)_{4}]^{2-}\) are diamagnetic while \([NiCl_{4}]^{2-}\) is paramagnetic.

The value of \(n\) is the total number of electrons transferred in the BALANCED reaction.

Oxidation half: in \(BH_{4}^{-}\) hydrogen is hydridic \((-1)\) and boron is \(+3\); in \(H_{2}BO_{3}^{-}\) boron is still \(+3\), so the electrons come from the four hydride hydrogens going to \(+1\):

\(BH_{4}^{-} + 3H_{2}O \rightarrow H_{2}BO_{3}^{-} + 8H^{+} + 8e^{-}\)

Reduction half: chlorine goes from \(+5\) in \(ClO_{3}^{-}\) to \(-1\) in \(Cl^{-}\), a 6-electron change:

\(ClO_{3}^{-} + 6H^{+} + 6e^{-} \rightarrow Cl^{-} + 3H_{2}O\)

To balance electrons take the LCM of 8 and 6, which is 24: multiply the oxidation half by 3 and the reduction half by 4.

\(3BH_{4}^{-} + 4ClO_{3}^{-} \rightarrow 3H_{2}BO_{3}^{-} + 4Cl^{-} + 3H_{2}O\)

Check: charge \(-7\) on both sides, atoms balanced. Electrons transferred \(= 3\times 8 = 4\times 6 = 24\), so \(n = 24\).
